title: AI Is Splitting Software Into Winners and Losers, Citi’s Tyler Radke Says
detail:
AI Is Splitting Software Into Winners and Losers, Citi’s Tyler Radke Says
Darryn Pollock
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 7:22 PM MST 2 min read
ADBE
MSFT
C
PLTR
SNOW
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Fed rate hikes stock sectors performance chart. Photo by BeInCrypto

Citi's Tyler Radke says AI is creating software winners and losers. He expects Microsoft's revenue growth to top 20% while Adobe feels pressure as AI projects absorb corporate budgets.

Radke, Citi's co-head of US software equity research, told Bloomberg Television the sector looked very different earlier this year. At that point, a chip stock at the bottom of its sector still beat software's top performer.

Who Are the Software Winners and Losers as AI Reshapes Budgets?

In the Bloomberg interview, Radke said AI is lifting growth at Microsoft, Palantir, and Snowflake, a cloud data company.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ubSzSCDBgGg

In contrast, Adobe and smaller application vendors face pressure as information technology (IT) budgets shift to AI, he said.

Microsoft anchors his case, with Office priced under $100 a month and bundling security and Copilot, its AI assistant.

Meanwhile, he says rivals charge hundreds of dollars monthly, which leaves Microsoft room to monetize further.

For context, Microsoft's revenue grew 18% in the quarter ended June 30.

Radke added that Citi's survey of chief information officers (CIOs) places Microsoft's in-house AI models near the leading labs.

Is Consolidation the Next Phase for Pressured Software Makers?

Salesforce offered a fresh example on Tuesday. A filing shows it agreed to buy Braze, a customer engagement platform, for $47.50 per share in cash.

Salesforce shares rose about 20% after its last quarterly report, Radke noted.

Even so, he says, the question after half a dozen large deals is whether Salesforce can speed up organic growth.

Moreover, higher financing costs could add to that pressure. Citi's neocloud debt thesis blames bond yields, not weak demand, for the selloff in AI cloud providers.

In addition, Radke said 2026 capacity at those providers is sold out, making a total AI bust hard to picture.

He expects scale to decide who survives, with larger providers likely to outlast smaller rivals if capital stays costly.

Katie Stockton, founder of research firm Fairlead Strategies, lists wider credit spreads among three stock warning signs.

If financing stays costly, the split Radke describes could widen, as strategic buyers and private equity firms target pressured makers.

Stablecoin Transfers Hit $891 Billion in Third Quarter: Report

Stablecoins moved more than $400 million an hour in adjusted transfer volume during the third quarter, according to a report commissioned by Coinbase (NASDAQ: $COIN). Quarterly activity reached $891 billion, more than quadruple the level of early 2023.

The report, conducted by The Block Research, found that 73% of screened stablecoin transfer volume took place outside U.S. banking hours, including nights, weekends and holidays. That round-the-clock pattern is a large part of the pitch for stablecoins over traditional payment rails, which shut down when banks do.

Banks and businesses appear to be taking notice. Seven of the 10 largest U.S. banks have tested stablecoins or tokenized deposits for settlement, the report found. Among mid-market companies doing cross-border business, 30% now use or are piloting stablecoins, up from 10% in 2024. Business-to-business payment volume rose 36% from a year earlier.

More From Cryptoprowl:

Cardano Founder Hoskinson Says Midnight Will Surpass Zcash, Urges Gemini to List ADA

Stacks Founder Warns Bitcoin Security Breach Could Hit Entire Crypto Market

Coinbase Targets Banks As Institutional Crypto Adoption Grows

60 Percent of Community Banks See Stablecoins as a Threat to Deposits, Lending

Crypto Heavyweights Back OKX at $25B Valuation

The researchers also counted 293 million blockchain addresses holding stablecoins, more than the combined number of cards issued by American Express (NYSE: $AXP) and Discover. They cautioned that an address does not necessarily equal a single user.

The report goes further and estimates what could happen if stablecoins took over most cross-border payments. Moving 80% of international transactions onto stablecoin networks could add $155 billion a year to global GDP and free roughly $3 trillion in liquidity that banks now hold to support cross-border payments. Those figures rest on hypothetical adoption scenarios, not gains that have been measured. The authors also acknowledged that widespread adoption could reduce bank lending, which might offset some of the benefits of faster, cheaper payments.

Consumer interest in bank-offered crypto is rising, too. A separate survey released Monday by the National Cryptocurrency Association found that 42% of U.S. adults, about 112 million people, would be more likely to open an account with a bank that offers crypto services or use that bank for more of their finances. Some 18% would like to buy or use stablecoins through their main bank. Banks have mostly stayed quiet, however: 64% of respondents said their bank, credit union or financial advisor had never brought up crypto, and 43% didn't know whether their bank offers it.

title: Morgan Stanley sees 32% Citigroup upside after brutal sell-off
detail:
Morgan Stanley sees 32% Citigroup upside after brutal sell-off
Mwangi Enos, Celine Provini
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 1:07 PM MST 5 min read
C
Trade C on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

I've followed bank stocks, and I've noticed some companies struggle to shake off their past, no matter how much progress they make. I think Citigroup is one of them, and I'll tell you why.

Whenever I look at the bank's turnaround efforts, I ask how much improvement it will take before Wall Street finally gives Citi some credit.

That tension was even more relevant on Oct. 13, after Citigroup reported its Q3 2026 earnings. Citi continues to perform better than its reputation suggests, yet Wall Street still seems reluctant to give the bank the credit it deserves.

Citigroup (C) reported Q3 2026 net income of $5.2 billion, up 17% from a year earlier. Revenue rose 7.9% to $23.8 billion, beating Wall Street's $23.74 billion consensus, while earnings per share jumped to $2.85 from $1.86 a year ago, according to Citi's Q3 earnings release.

Despite those strong results, Citigroup shares fell 6% to close at $124.53. C now trades at $121.69 as of the Oct. 19 close, up 5.86% year to date and 28.02% over the past year, according to Yahoo Finance.

Also Read: Citi spots troubling 1970s warning for U.S. stocks

Citi's earnings were strong, but the market reaction was puzzling

"[We saw] the best third-quarter revenue in a decade," CEO Jane Fraser said in the earnings release. Fraser noted 10 consecutive quarters of year-over-year positive operating leverage and full-year ROTCE guidance raised to above 11%, ahead of the original 10% to 11% target. 

The efficiency ratio is now expected to be below 60%. Services delivered another standout quarter of revenue up 15%. Equities are up 14%, and Wealth Management is delivering returns above 14%, according to Citi's Q3 earnings release.

Still, the stock dropped 6%.

Related: This bank has more upside than JP Morgan: Stocks to buy after earnings

Morgan Stanley's note, shared with me at TheStreet on Oct. 14, described the reaction as "puzzling" and said the bank and several investors were similarly confused. The firm reiterated its Overweight rating and $164 price target, implying roughly 32% upside from the then-current levels.

The note is worth taking seriously because of the specific concern Morgan Stanley raised. It explains the gap between what Citigroup reported and how the market priced it.

The real tension on Citi is the sequential decline before the next catalyst

Morgan Stanley identified three overlapping reasons for the sell-off, none of which individually justifies a 6% decline, but which together created a vacuum of near-term catalysts.

First: Q4 ROTCE is expected to decline sequentially from Q3, with management flagging market seasonality that could push revenues down more than 20% quarter over quarter.

Citi Research named Aave the go-to lending layer for tokenized collateral, yet AAVE sits 77% below its $662 all-time high.

JPMorgan's Kinexys Tokenized Collateral Network competes directly with Aave for institutional flows, and AAVE plays no role in Horizon's lending operations.

AAVE's recovery requires a named institution to publicly commit tokenized collateral to Horizon and push the token back above its recent $188 high.

Citi Research, part of Citigroup (NYSE: C), has identified Aave (CRYPTO: AAVE) as a potential leader in lending for tokenized assets once they move on-chain. The Citi Aave note highlights the importance of collateral mobility as one of the key benefits of tokenization. Collateral mobility allows users to pledge tokenized assets—like a blockchain version of Treasury funds—as loan security without the delays of traditional bank systems.

Aave operates as a lending protocol, enabling users to borrow cryptocurrencies by locking up their assets as collateral. Citi's interest positions Aave as one of the few decentralized finance (DeFi) applications a major bank has publicly named as possible plumbing for tokenized markets.

Thapana_Studio / Shutterstock.com

Despite this endorsement, AAVE continues to struggle. As of October 20, 2026, the token trades at $148, down 7.4% over the past week and 2.1% in the last 24 hours. Moreover, it is now down 77% from its May 2021 peak of $662.

While public summaries of Citi's report do not specify a price target for AAVE or name any banks or funds that have committed to using Aave, the question remains: Can Wall Street's support for Aave's framework help the token regain lost value?

Citi's Thesis Points Straight at Aave's Horizon Market

Citi's analysis focuses on a service Aave has already built. On August 26, 2025, Aave Labs, the protocol's primary developer, launched Aave Horizon. This lending market operates on Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and allows institutions and qualified users to borrow stablecoins—tokens tied to the U.S. dollar—against real-world assets.

In Horizon, real-world assets refer to tokenized funds containing U.S. Treasury bills and AAA-rated collateralized loan obligations—bundles of corporate loans categorized by risk. Initial collateral options were provided by Superstate and Centrifuge, with Horizon collaborating with Ripple and VanEck.
